lesson.title: Good data, fair AI
lesson.subtitle: Why AI can work better for some people than others

video.title: Good data, fair AI
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
A colleague at Salma’s school — appears in the hook; we see his words on the phone, no voice
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Why does it get me wrong?

scenes.visual: Staff room, afternoon. Salma speaks into her phone. On screen: ‘Mass chest moved to Thursday’ with a wavy underline. She tries again, slower — wrong again. She hands the phone to a colleague; he speaks once and the text appears correctly. Salma looks at the camera, one eyebrow up.
scenes.animation: Text types on letter by letter; the wrong words wobble (150 ms). Quick push-in on Salma’s face.
scenes.narration: “Maths test moved to Thursday.” … It wrote “mass chest”? Again! My colleague says the same words — perfect, first time. So what’s wrong with my voice?
scenes.sound: Phone ‘ding’; a soft comic ‘boing’ on the wrong words.
scenes.vids: Phone close-up as a flat illustration. Put the phone text in Vids text boxes; translators write a gentle local mishearing. Character: Salma, illustrated secondary maths teacher, ink outlines.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: why AI can work better for some people than others — and how to fix it.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: Salma’s phone in the centre. Behind it, a big stack of sound-wave cards (recordings) slides in: almost all one colour and pattern, a few in a second colour with stripes. A sparkle forms over the big group. Salma’s striped sound wave arrives, and the phone shows a small question mark.
scenes.animation: Cards stack in 2 s; sparkle pulses once; question mark pops (150 ms).
scenes.on_screen_text: Whose voices did it learn from?
scenes.narration: Nothing is wrong with Salma’s voice. Voice typing learned from recordings of speech. If most came from a few accents, it works best for voices like those — and makes more mistakes with voices that were rare.
scenes.sound: Soft whoosh as the cards stack.
scenes.vids: Sound-wave cards: rounded rectangles with a wave line, no text. Show the two groups by colour and stripes, so it still works in black and white.

scenes.visual: Two tall columns of 100 small tiles, side by side, with an illustrated speaker under each: a Black speaker and a white speaker. In the left column, 35 tiles flip to a cross; in the right column, 19 tiles flip. A small ‘2020’ tag sits in the corner.
scenes.animation: Tiles flip in quick waves, about 1 s per column. No other motion.
scenes.narration: This happens with real tools. In a 2020 US study, speech tools from five big companies got about 35 words wrong in 100 for Black speakers, and 19 for white speakers.
scenes.sound: Light ticks as the tiles flip.
scenes.vids: Build the columns with Vids shapes. Draw both speakers with equal care, in everyday clothes; no stereotypes. No company names or logos.

scenes.visual: Clean definition card on white with the AI track chip. Left: a balance scale tipping to one side (bias). Right: a box of example cards with one piece missing (data gap).
scenes.animation: Scale tips slowly (400 ms); the gap where the piece is missing blinks once.
scenes.narration: When an AI system works worse for some groups of people than for others, we call it bias. It often starts with a data gap: some people, places, accents or languages are missing or rare in the examples.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: Salma at her desk, marking homework. A page shows a 1 written with a long stroke at the top; she frowns and marks it as 7. A few pages later, the same style — now she reads it correctly and smiles.
scenes.animation: Pages turn; a small sparkle near Salma on the last page.
scenes.narration: Think of marking homework. A new pupil writes her ones with a long top stroke, so you read them as sevens. You weren’t unfair — you’d never seen that style. A few examples later, it’s easy.
scenes.vids: Draw the numbers large and simple so they read at 240p. The new pupil appears only as her homework page.

scenes.visual: Salma holds a phone clipped to a small microscope, eyebrow raised. Two big answer cards drop in: ‘With the kind it learned from’ and ‘With other kinds’.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A malaria app learned mostly from one kind of parasite. Where will it make more mistakes?
scenes.sound: Two gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The ‘With other kinds’ card gets a blue check badge. Cut to a lab bench: a phone clipped to a microscope shows a blood sample, and small boxes appear around a few dots. A lab worker looks closely and nods.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Boxes draw on one by one.
scenes.narration: Other kinds — and it’s a real case. In Uganda, Makerere University researchers are testing a malaria tool trained mainly on the most common parasite there. It needs more examples to find the others.
scenes.vids: Blue for correct (never green), always with the check icon. Lab scene: flat illustration, no logos; the phone screen shows simple dots, not a real medical image.

scenes.visual: A grid of illustrated portrait cards with many skin tones. A scan line passes; cross badges appear far more often on darker-skinned women’s cards. Small flag pins show Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Iceland, Finland and Sweden. Then the scan runs again and fewer crosses appear.
scenes.animation: Scan line sweeps once (1 s); badges pop (150 ms); crosses fade on the second sweep.
scenes.narration: In 2018, researchers tested face tools that guess gender, using photos of members of parliament from Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa and northern Europe. The tools were wrong for up to about one in three darker-skinned women, but under one in 100 lighter-skinned men. Within months, the companies improved them.
scenes.sound: Soft scanner hum; gentle chime as crosses fade.
scenes.vids: Respectful illustrated portraits only — never photos of real MPs. Flags as small pins. Make badges large enough to read at 240p.

scenes.visual: Four cards flip in, one by one: a group of people with a plus sign; a checklist beside three different faces; a megaphone; an eye beside a hand. Then a short montage: volunteers of different ages recording their voices on phones and writing sentences in their own languages.
scenes.animation: Cards flip in 300 ms apart. Montage cuts every 1.5 s.
scenes.on_screen_text: Four ways to fix a gap
scenes.narration: How do we fix a gap? Collect examples from the people and places where a tool will be used. Test it with different groups. Let people report mistakes, and keep humans checking. Groups like Masakhane — “we build together” — are collecting African-language examples.
scenes.vids: Use flat icons from the Darsi set on white cards. Volunteers: varied ages and settings, everyday clothes; no logos or readable screens.

scenes.visual: A phone shows two piles of message bubbles: ‘Safe message’ and ‘Scam’. Every bubble has the same small striped dot (one language). A new bubble with a different dotted mark slides in, and a question mark appears over it.
scenes.animation: Bubbles stack in 1 s; the new bubble slides in; the question mark pulses once.
scenes.on_screen_text: Your turn: train a scam spotter
scenes.narration: After the video, try it: train a tiny scam spotter with English messages, then test it with a Kiswahili scam. Watch what it guesses — and ask why.
scenes.vids: Mock the phone screen with Vids shapes. Show each language by mark and pattern, never colour alone. No real app names.

scenes.visual: Salma holds up her phone, smiling now. Two big answer cards drop in: ‘More recordings of the same voices’ and ‘Recordings of voices like Salma’s’.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Voice typing makes more mistakes with my accent. Which fix helps most?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight ‘Recordings of voices like Salma’s’.

scenes.visual: The ‘Recordings of voices like Salma’s’ card gets the check badge. The screen resolves into three summary cards: a stack of example cards, a puzzle with one piece missing, and a group of different people.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Voices like Salma’s — yes! AI is only as good as its examples. Gaps often mean more mistakes for the people left out. It’s not just how many examples — it’s whose.
scenes.vids: Hold the three cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Salma’s classroom. Pupils stick fruit drawings in a big box on the board: many mangoes, bananas and oranges. Salma holds up a local fruit nobody drew. Pupils point at the closest drawing, then laugh and start talking. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Check before you trust’.
scenes.animation: Drawings fly from pupils’ hands to the board. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: pupils draw fruit to “train” a pretend recogniser. Then show a local fruit nobody drew. What was missing? And how is that like voice typing and accents?
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. Draw the fruit simply. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: A malaria app learned mostly from one kind of parasite. Where will it make more mistakes?

options.text: With the kind it learned from

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it saw few examples of other kinds, so the patterns it learned fit them less well.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it saw many examples of that kind. Mistakes happen more with the kinds it rarely saw.

checkpoints.prompt: Voice typing makes more mistakes with Salma’s accent. Which fix helps most?

options.text: More recordings of the same voices

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the gap is about whose voices were missing. Recordings of voices like hers fill it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — more of the same voices doesn’t fill the gap. It needs examples of voices like Salma’s.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3 minute 47 second animated explainer video for teachers titled “Good data, fair AI”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a sunny yellow (#ffc53d) accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Salma, a careful, funny secondary maths teacher. Follow the attached script scene by scene: voice typing gets Salma’s words wrong but works for a colleague; whose voices it learned from; a 2020 speech study; bias and data gaps; a handwriting analogy; a malaria tool trained on one kind of parasite; a 2018 face-tool test; four ways to fix a data gap; a scam-spotter lab preview; two quick quiz pauses; end with a classroom fruit activity. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene.
